extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemaking staff, regulatory analysts, and policymakers (oil & gas NESHAP rulemaking participants)
extracted.subtask_short: NESHAP residual risk and MACT comment
extracted.subtask_description: A public-comment critique of EPA's proposed NESHAP (residual risk and MACT) for oil and natural gas production and natural gas transmission and storage, focusing on data currency, missing sources/pollutants, modeling methods, cost assumptions, and the MACT technology review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of most recent emissions data
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA failed to use more recent emission data than the 2005 NEI for the section 112(f)(2) and section 112(d)(6) proposed actions; EPA should use the most recent NEI (e.g., 2008 NEI) or collect more recent data from the source categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the proposal is dated August 23, 2011, it is perplexing that EPA failed to use more recent emission data than the 2005 NEI... Using the 2005 NEI does not reflect current conditions in either of these two source categories given the significant changes, particularly in on-shore gas production due to shale and other gas plays. EPA appears to use the 2008 NEI in its Regulatory Impact Analysis; thus the 2008 NEI was available and should have been used as a starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect source-specific updated data rather than rely on legacy datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should collect more recent data directly from the source categories rather than relying on older legacy datasets (e.g., 1998/1999 MACT data or pre-2005 NEI) and must explain why legacy datasets are representative if used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA could have collected more recent data from the source categories. It is unclear why EPA did not do so. For small glycol dehydrators, EPA relied on data from the 1998 legacy docket and asserted representativeness without adequate support. Such assertions are specious without further support given industry changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure NEI/data represent current industry conditions (shale plays etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data used must reflect current industry conditions, including changes from unconventional and shale plays that significantly alter sources, emissions, and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2005 NEI likely reflects data from prior to 2005 and is not representative of current industry conditions. There has been a continued increase in gas production from onshore nonconventional gas plays (e.g., Barnett, Marcellus, Eagle Ford, Haynesville), so using 2005 NEI is insufficient and flawed given growth since 2005.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on ECHO to update or validate NEI coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-checking NEI with EPA's ECHO enforcement database is not sufficient to ensure representativeness or completeness of facilities and emissions, particularly for new sources from shale plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's ECHO database contains fewer facilities than the NEI for these categories and likely misses numerous new sources; therefore ECHO is inadequate as a benchmark and cannot substitute for comprehensive data collection or update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensively identify and evaluate all HAP-emitting sources at major facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should start with a comprehensive set of HAP-emitting sources at 'major source' facilities in the affected source categories and, based on technical arguments and current data, select all HAP sources that should be covered under the NESHAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA provides no explanation why the proposed rule fails to cover numerous other HAP-emitting sources. Examples of missing or improperly addressed sources include offshore platforms; combustion sources (engines, turbines, heater treaters); process vents; fugitive emissions from wells, drilling, pipeline pigging, waste pits; leaks from compressors, pumps, valves; chemical injection pumps; pneumatic devices; well deliquefaction processes; produced water sources (pits, ponds); flares; compressor station blowdowns; storage vessels associated with transmission and storage; truck unloading vapors; landfarming; pipeline leaks; venting for maintenance; and operational malfunction releases (e.g., pressure relief device releases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume NSPS satisfies Section 112 duties
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA cannot rely on an NSPS (section 111) standard to fulfill its duty to regulate Hazardous Air Pollutants under section 112, because NSPS may only cover new/modified sources and may not cover all relevant sources or HAPs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NSPS, to the extent it covers these sources, is limited to new and modified sources and may not cover existing sources of HAPs. EPA must provide a thorough discussion if it believes NSPS coverage obviates section 112 regulation and demonstrate that such NESHAPs have been updated in accordance with section 112(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly consider fugitive and malfunction emissions (acute and SSM events)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must evaluate fugitive emissions and emissions during malfunctions (e.g., blow-outs, startup/shutdown/malfunction (SSM) events) for health risk assessments and ensure these are addressed in the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most emissions from listed sources are fugitive. Significant HAPs are released during malfunctions. While elimination of the SSM exemption is appropriate, it is not clear how health risk from HAP emissions during malfunctions (e.g., blow-outs) are specifically addressed. EPA should assess HAP emissions from operational malfunctions and pressure relief device releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on surrogate-based HAP estimates without supporting analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When HAP emission estimates are developed by surrogacy from VOC estimates, EPA must provide analysis and data supporting the surrogacy assumptions rather than assuming fixed VOC-to-HAP ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 983 of 1,318 facilities, emission estimates for key HAPs were not available in the NEI and EPA developed surrogate estimates based on reported VOC emission estimates and VOC percent ratios; EPA provides no analysis or data to support this surrogacy assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider HAPs identified in local and docket studies, not just NEI summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider additional HAP information available in the docket and local studies (e.g., Sublette County, DISH Texas), which identify HAPs not necessarily reflected in NEI-based summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sublette County Air Toxics project reported many HAPs at monitoring sites; DISH, Texas resident sampling confirmed benzene, carbon disulfide, carbonyl sulfide, naphthalene, and xylene in excess of screening levels. EPA should incorporate such data into its pollutant list and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include produced water constituents (HAPs and radionuclides) in pollutant assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should consider HAPs (e.g., organic acids, PAHs, phenols, volatiles like acetone and methanol) and possible radionuclides present in produced water when identifying pollutants for regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produced water can contain hydrocarbons, low molecular weight carboxylic acids, ketones, alcohols, and sometimes high radionuclide concentrations (e.g., radium-226 in Marcellus produced water). These are HAPs and should be considered in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk review must use representative and current emissions data (not NATA/NEI 2005 alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's residual risk assessment should not rely on outdated datasets (e.g., 2005 NATA/NEI) as the sole basis for modeling and risk conclusions; data must be representative of emissions today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The risk review relies on older data (2005 NEI). Given industry changes since 2005, these data cannot be assumed representative of emissions in 2011. EPA must provide support for representativeness or use updated data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and disclose industry-supplied updates and dataset changes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the NEI or other datasets were 'updated with industry supplied data,' EPA must document where such updates were used, what changes were made, and which industry sources supplied the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA stated the NEI was updated with industry-supplied data to identify limitations and issues, but the record does not indicate where such data were used or what was changed; transparency is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple years of meteorological data for dispersion modeling (ideally up to five years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Site-specific dispersion modeling should employ multiple years (up to five) of meteorological data to capture variability; modeling using a single year (EPA typically used 1991) is insufficient to represent long-term conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In HEM-AERMOD, ideally up to five years of data are used; EPA modeled only a single year (typically 1991) due to insufficient formatted input files. One year may under- or over-predict long-term ambient levels and is not justified as representative for 2011.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure meteorological station representativeness and consider terrain, distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting the 'nearest' NWS station as representative is inadequate without considering terrain, land/water features, and the actual distance (average 40 miles in EPA's analysis) from the facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA selected nearest stations with an average distance of 40 miles (72 km). Meteorological data are influenced by terrain and local features; EPA must justify representativeness or use closer/site-specific measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify short-term emission multipliers used to estimate one-hour peaks
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's assumption that maximum one-hour emission rate equals 10 times average annual hourly rate must be justified with data that adequately captures high-emission events (e.g., blowouts, well development), not only routine variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA applied a factor of ten based on limited Texas data collected in 2001 and stated it covers routinely-variable emissions and SSM. There is no basis that this covers extreme events; EPA should show the data set includes events like blowouts or evaluate different multipliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model acute exposures at appropriate near-field locations and meteorology
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term (one-hour) concentrations should be estimated at realistic near-facility locations, with local meteorology, and not rely on distant stations and generalized multipliers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA estimated worst-case short-term concentrations at census block centroids and at points no nearer than 100 meters from facility centers and used distant meteorological data and the 10x multiplier—this likely underestimates acute risk at the fenceline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use up-to-date population data (2010 Census) for centroid-based exposure modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating concentrations at census block centroids for long-term exposures, EPA should use 2010 census data (not 2000) to reflect current population patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used the 2000 Census centroids; there is no discussion of sensitivity given availability of 2010 data; EPA should use 2010 Census.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a full accounting of emission sources included in facility-wide risk analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must disclose which sources (including combustion and other identified types) were included in facility-wide risk modeling and ensure all relevant sources were modeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA stated it estimated maximum inhalation cancer and chronic non-cancer risks associated with all HAP emissions at the facility, including sources not part of the source categories, but did not specify whether combustion sources or other identified emission types (pipeline pigging, produced water, etc.) were included. Tables show very limited PAH entries, suggesting omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include combustion sources in emissions and risk tables where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should include combustion-related HAP emissions (e.g., PAHs, formaldehyde, 1,3-butadiene) from engines, turbines, heaters, etc., in emissions inventories and risk calculations for production and transmission facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables in the residual risk report contain PAH emissions from just a few facilities; most production and transmission facilities will have combustion sources emitting PAHs and other HAPs, and these appear undercounted or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support cost-effectiveness scaling assumptions between small and large units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must provide evidence for assumptions that cost-effectiveness for larger units will not exceed some multiple of small units (e.g., 'not to exceed twice'), since economies of scale often make larger units more cost-effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assumed cost-effectiveness for large glycol dehydrators would not exceed twice that of small units without support; the record provides no basis for this and scaling can work in the opposite direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify assumed control efficiencies (e.g., 95%) and analyze alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must justify assumed control efficiencies for control devices (e.g., 95% for condensers/combustors or closed vent + control) and analyze the cost-effectiveness impact of higher efficiencies (98-99%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assumed 95% HAP reduction for condensers/combustors and for closed vent + control configurations but did not explain why 95% rather than 98-99% was used or evaluate cost impacts of greater efficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume equal costs for multiple control devices without support
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the cost of a second control device equals the first device requires justification; control device cost depends on process size, gas volumes, contaminant concentrations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assumed the costs for the second device equal the first for dehydrators and storage vessels but provided no support; this is questionable because costs vary with process conditions and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a wider range of control technologies (including high-efficiency options)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA should evaluate additional control approaches (e.g., fixed-roof tanks routed to carbon adsorbers or thermal/catalytic oxidizers, internal floating roofs routed to adsorbers/oxidizers) that may achieve 99%+ destruction of HAPs and have been applied in related sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA listed cover + closed vent + control devices and second devices but should also consider other feasible, high-efficiency approaches used in refineries and similar sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume fraction of VOC that are HAPs without supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions such as HAPs making up approximately 1/20 of VOCs (leading to LDAR cost-effectiveness being ~20x greater for HAPs than VOCs) must be supported by data; poor HAP data makes such assumptions unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relied on NSPS LDAR analyses and assumed HAPs are ~1/20 of VOCs, but given poor HAP data support for fugitive sources, this ratio is not defensible without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: MACT (section 112(d)(6)) technology review must consider broad 'developments'
rubrics_metrics.description: For the MACT review, 'developments' should include any add-on control technology or equipment not considered in MACT development, improvements in previously considered controls that could yield significant additional reductions, and work practices/operational procedures not previously considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA defined 'development' narrowly in the NSPS review; for MACT, EPA must consider a broad set of developments across processes/practices/control techniques and not limit analysis to a few sources (e.g., dehydrators, storage vessels, fugitive emissions) when many other sources exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a comprehensive assessment of all HAP emission points before finalizing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalizing the NESHAP, EPA should perform a thorough assessment of all HAP emission points across the affected source categories to identify gaps and ensure sufficient protection of community air quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on omissions in data, missing sources, surrogate assumptions, and modeling flaws, EPA's proposal contains significant gaps; a comprehensive assessment is necessary to ensure the rule adequately protects public health.
